narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Soukous originated in the 1960s, evolving from Congolese rumba.
It was pioneered by bands like Orchestre Sinza Kotoko in Brazzaville and later refined by groups like Zaïko Langa Langa in Kinshasa, who accelerated the tempo and emphasized the sebene.
on_screen: Map: Democratic Republic of the Congo · Africa

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Soukous is a celebratory genre used for social gatherings.
It has served as a vehicle for both political expression and personal storytelling, with lyrics covering themes of love, struggle, and success.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by energetic hip movements and shifting body weight.
It features freestyle sections that encourage audience participation, often performed at high speeds to match the rapid guitar-driven sebene.
Watch for Hip movement.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (XS4ErzpF9uw)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Freestyle, individual or group.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The genre utilizes electric guitars, double bass, congas, and brass/woodwinds.
The lead guitar is central, often playing in higher registers, while the bass provides a 16th-note rhythmic foundation.
Listen for the Electric guitar, Double bass, Congas, Brass.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 128 beats a minute.
Characterized by rapid, intricate electric guitar solos in the higher registers and a driving, percussive bassline.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Marie-Louise — Antoine Wendo Kolosoy; Kiri-Kiri Mabina Ya Sika — Docteur Nico

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically associated with dance halls and urban clubs in Kinshasa and Brazzaville, soukous is a staple of weddings and public festivals.
Fashion and elegance, particularly within the Sapeur movement, are integral to the performance culture.
on_screen: Image gallery: 8 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Franco Luambo, Tabu Ley Rochereau, Docteur Nico, Papa Wemba, and Aurlus Mabélé.
Variants include the fast-paced 'ndombolo', the 'kiri-kiri' dance style, and the Colombian 'champeta', which incorporates soukous rhythms.
Soukous is a direct descendant of Congolese rumba, which itself was influenced by Cuban son and local maringa dance music.
